issuing_body: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
title: 2019 First Special Session, Chapter 9, Article 2, Section 107 — CCAP Administrative Disqualification
supports: Section 107 added a separate administrative-disqualification procedure for child-care providers accused of intentional program violations when a criminal action had not been pursued.

Intentional program violations included intentional false or misleading statements, intentional concealment or withholding of facts, and repeated intentional violations of CCAP/program-integrity regulations.
The law stated that intent may be proven in the administrative proceeding by demonstrating a pattern of conduct that violates program rules.
On appeal, the issuing agency bears the burden to prove the intentional program violation by a preponderance of the evidence.
A provider administratively disqualified under the new procedure was disqualified from CCAP payments for three years for the first offense and permanently for a subsequent offense.

Section 107 contains no separate effective-date clause; under Minn. Stat. § 645.02, a nonappropriation act without a different specified date generally takes effect August 1 following final enactment.
selected_locators: Chapter 9, Article 2, Sec. 107, new Minn. Stat. § 256.046, subd. 3(a) — intentional program violation and pattern evidence
Sec. 107, subd. 3(e) — preponderance burden on appeal
Minn. Stat. § 645.02 — default effective date rule
important_qualifications: This change did not lower the burden of proof for a Minnesota criminal conviction. It created an administrative-disqualification remedy used in lieu of a criminal action when criminal prosecution had not been pursued.

The preponderance standard belongs to the administrative appeal described by the statute, not to a criminal prosecution, where the constitutional beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard remains applicable.
Later recodification and amendments moved CCAP program-integrity provisions; publication about 2019 conduct should cite this historical session law rather than only today's section numbering.
